big: Meena spends ₹50,000 a month today. She thinks she needs ₹50,000 a month when she retires in 25 years. At 6% inflation, the same life will cost about ₹2.15 lakh a month.

lines: I will retire at 60. How do I even know what number to aim for?
Start with what you spend now, grow it by inflation to the year you retire, then see how big a pot can pay that for life.

small: a month in 25 years, if prices rise 6% a year
alt: Bars showing a monthly expense of fifty thousand rupees rising over twenty-five years, in thousands
caps: At 6% a year, ten years on, the same life costs about ₹90,000.
After twenty-five years, about ₹2.15 lakh. An assumed rate, not a forecast.

h: A rule of thumb for the pot
intro: A made-up example, to show the idea.
note: The 25-times rule matches drawing about 4% a year. It is a rule of thumb and not a promise.

q: Rohan spends ₹40,000 a month and will retire in 20 years. What is wrong with planning for ₹40,000 then?
opts: Retirees never spend anything on food or travel
Savings grow by themselves to cover all of it
The bank will pay his monthly bills for him
Prices will rise, so the same life costs more
why: Retirees still spend on food, health and daily needs, so costs do not vanish.
Savings grow only if they are invested well, and not by themselves.
A bank does not pay a retiree's bills, so the plan must cover them.
Inflation lifts prices every year, so the same life needs a bigger monthly sum.

opts: The chance that markets rise for many years
The chance of outliving your savings
The risk of losing a job before sixty
The risk of a loan growing in size
why: Rising markets are good news and not a risk to your savings.
Living longer than planned means savings must last for more years.
Job loss is a risk to earning years, not the years after retirement.
A loan growing is a different risk and not about the length of life.

q: A retiree withdraws far more than the plan allows in the first years. What is likely?
opts: The corpus grows faster, since money is moving
Inflation stops for the whole period
The corpus may run out before life ends
The withdrawal rate has no effect on the pot
why: Money withdrawn no longer earns, so the pot grows slower and not faster.
Inflation goes on whatever the retiree does with the withdrawals.
Heavy early draws shrink the pot, leaving less to earn and to last.
The rate of withdrawal matters a lot to how long the pot lasts.

q: Meena's yearly spend at retirement is ₹10 lakh. Using the 25-times rule, what pot does it point to?
why: Ten lakh times twenty-five is ₹2.5 crore, matching a draw of about 4%.
₹25 lakh is only two and a half years of her spending.
₹10 crore is forty times her yearly spend, far above the rule.
₹1 crore would last about ten years at her spending.

pts: Grow today's spending by inflation to find the cost at retirement.
A pot of about 25 times yearly spend is a rule of thumb, not a promise.
Longevity risk is outliving your savings, so plan for a long life.
